title: LSM Trees vs B-Trees
description: Compare the two dominant storage engine data structures: write amplification in B-trees, space amplification in LSM trees, bloom filters, compaction strategies, and when to choose RocksDB vs InnoDB.

segments.text: Every database stores data using one of two fundamental structures: B-trees or LSM trees. B-trees power PostgreSQL and MySQL InnoDB. LSM trees power RocksDB, Cassandra, and LevelDB. Each makes a fundamentally different tradeoff between read performance, write performance, and space usage.

A B-tree maintains sorted data in fixed-size pages, typically 8 to 16 kilobytes. Reads are fast: traverse the tree from root to leaf in O(log N) page reads. For a table with one billion rows and a branching factor of 500, you need only four page reads. With the top three levels cached, every lookup is a single disk read.

B-tree writes are the problem. Updating a single key requires reading the page, modifying it, and writing the entire page back. Even changing one byte rewrites 8 kilobytes. This is write amplification. Worse, splits cascade upward when pages are full. In InnoDB, random updates to a large table can produce a write amplification factor of 10 to 30.

LSM trees take the opposite approach. All writes go to an in-memory buffer called a memtable, usually a red-black tree or skip list. When the memtable fills up, typically at 64 megabytes, it's flushed to disk as an immutable sorted file called an SSTable. Writes are always sequential appends. No random I/O at all.

LSM tree reads are the tradeoff. To find a key, you check the memtable first, then search each SSTable level from newest to oldest. Without optimization, reads could check dozens of files. This is where bloom filters save the day: a probabilistic filter that tells you if a key is definitely NOT in a file, with a configurable false positive rate around one percent.
segments.thought_prompt: If each SSTable has a 1% bloom filter false positive rate and you have 10 SSTables, what's the expected number of unnecessary disk reads per lookup?

segments.text: Compaction merges SSTables to reclaim space and reduce read amplification. Leveled compaction, used by LevelDB, maintains size-bounded levels where each level is 10x the previous. Each key exists in exactly one file per level. This gives excellent read performance but high write amplification because data is rewritten across levels.

Tiered compaction, used by Cassandra, allows multiple files per level and merges all files in a tier at once. Lower write amplification because data moves through fewer levels. But higher space amplification because duplicate keys exist across tiers. Tiered is better for write-heavy workloads; leveled is better for read-heavy ones.

Space amplification is the LSM tree's hidden cost. With leveled compaction in RocksDB, space amplification is typically 1.1x, meaning 10 percent overhead. With tiered compaction, it can reach 2x or more because old versions coexist until compaction. For a one-terabyte dataset, that's an extra terabyte of wasted space.

RocksDB, created by Facebook, is the most widely used LSM engine. It powers MySQL's MyRocks storage engine, TiKV in TiDB, and CockroachDB's storage layer. In Facebook's benchmarks, MyRocks uses 50 percent less storage than InnoDB for the same data because LSM compression is more effective on sorted, immutable files.

Choose B-trees when your workload is read-heavy with random point lookups. When you need predictable latency without compaction storms. When you need strong transaction isolation — B-tree page locking is well understood. PostgreSQL and InnoDB handle OLTP workloads with mixed reads and writes extremely well up to moderate write volumes.

Choose LSM trees when writes dominate: time-series data, event logging, write-heavy analytics. When you need better compression ratios to reduce storage costs. When you can tolerate occasional compaction latency spikes. Cassandra processes millions of writes per second on LSM trees at Netflix, handling viewing history for 200 million subscribers.
segments.thought_prompt: For a time-series monitoring system ingesting 1M metrics/second with 90-day retention, would you choose B-tree or LSM?

segments.text: There's no universally better data structure. B-trees optimize for reads at the cost of write amplification. LSM trees optimize for writes at the cost of read amplification and compaction overhead. Know your workload's read-write ratio, latency requirements, and storage budget, then choose accordingly. The best engineers understand both deeply.
